intro: Practice, not a grade. Ten Regents-style questions on documents from this unit. Pick an answer and you'll see right away if it's right.

stimulus.content:
Arthur Young was a well-known writer on farming who supported enclosure. In 1801 he wrote:
“. . . the fact is, that by nineteen enclosure bills in twenty they [the poor] are injured, in some grossly injured. . . .”
stimulus.citation: Arthur Young, An Inquiry into the Propriety of Applying Wastes to the Better Maintenance and Support of the Poor, 1801

items.question: According to Arthur Young, how did most enclosure bills affect the poor?

choices.text: They gave the poor more common land
They harmed the poor, some of them badly
They had no real effect on the poor
They helped the poor buy their own farms

hints: Young gives a number: nineteen bills out of twenty. Reread what he says happens to the poor in them.
The word “injured” means harmed.
items.reasoning: Young says that in nineteen enclosure bills out of twenty the poor are injured, and in some grossly injured. Enclosure fenced off the common land where poor families grazed their animals.

items.question: Young's statement is strong evidence of the harm enclosure did because Young

choices.text: had lost his own family's farm to enclosure
wrote it before any enclosure acts passed
worked in a Manchester cotton mill
supported enclosure himself

hints: Read the line above the quotation before you read the quotation.
When someone admits a cost of the thing they support, that admission counts for more.
items.reasoning: The line above the quotation says Young supported enclosure. A supporter admitting that the poor were harmed is speaking against his own side, which makes his admission hard to dismiss.

items.document: Document — Edward Baines on England's position

stimulus.content: In comparing the advantages of England for manufactures with those of other countries, we can by no means overlook the excellent commercial position of the country — intermediate between the north and south of Europe; and its insular situation [island location], which, combined with the command of the seas, secures our territory from invasion or annoyance. The German ocean, the Baltic, and the Mediterranean are the regular highways for our ships; and our western ports command an unobstructed [clear] passage to the Atlantic, and to every quarter [part] of the world.
stimulus.citation: Edward Baines, History of the Cotton Manufacture in Great Britain, A. M. Kelley

items.question: Baines says England's position helped its manufacturing because England

choices.text: was an island that ruled the seas, with routes to the world
shared a long land border with Germany and the Baltic states
sat far from Europe and stayed out of its trade
needed no ports, since its goods moved by canal

hints: Find the two advantages Baines names: where England sits, and what kind of land it is.
“Insular situation” means island location.
items.reasoning: Baines points to England's position between the north and south of Europe and its island location. Together with command of the seas, that kept England safe and gave its ships clear routes to every part of the world.

choices.text: geographic context of Britain's Industrial Revolution

hints: Is Baines writing about when and what came before, or about where and why there?
Seas, ports and an island location are all about place.
items.reasoning: Baines describes where England is and why that place helped it manufacture and trade. Geographic context answers where it happened and why there.

items.question: Based on this document and your knowledge of social studies, ships sailing from England's western ports brought back

choices.text: silk from Japan for the weavers in British towns
coal from Germany to fuel the mills in British cities
raw cotton from the West Indies and the American South
iron ore from India for the forges of Birmingham

hints: Baines says the western ports open onto the Atlantic. What lies across the Atlantic?
Think about what Britain's cloth mills needed most.
items.reasoning: Britain's ships brought in raw cotton, first from the West Indies and later from the American South, and carried British goods all over the world. Both lie across the Atlantic from the western ports.

items.document: Document — Adam Smith on the division of labour

stimulus.content: “[A worker alone] could scarce, perhaps, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day. . . . The important business of making a pin is, in this manner, divided into about eighteen distinct operations. . . . I have seen a small manufactory [factory] of this kind where ten men only were employed. . . . Those ten persons, therefore, could make among them upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day.”
stimulus.citation: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776 (adapted)

items.question: According to Smith, ten workers could make more than forty-eight thousand pins a day because

choices.text: new steam-powered machines made each pin by itself
the government paid them for every pin
each of them worked twenty hours a day
the job was split into about eighteen operations

hints: Smith never mentions a machine. Reread how he says the work is done.
Find the number eighteen.
items.reasoning: Smith says the business of making a pin is divided into about eighteen distinct operations. One worker alone could hardly make one pin a day; ten workers splitting the steps made more than 48,000.

items.question: The idea Smith describes in this passage is called

choices.text: laissez-faire
division of labor
enclosure
the domestic system

hints: Smith is describing how a job is split up, not what government should do.
Look under The words in the unit review for splitting a job into small steps.
items.reasoning: Division of labor means splitting a job into small steps, each done by a different worker. Laissez-faire is Smith's other idea: that government should stay out of business.

items.document: Document — Edmund Cartwright and the power loom

stimulus.content:
. . .Once back in Leicestershire, however, Cartwright found that the idea of devising a weaving machine had lodged itself firmly in his mind.
“It struck me,” he wrote, “that as in plain weaving, according to the conception I then had of the business, that as there could only be three movements which were to follow each other in succession, there would be little difficulty in reproducing and repeating them.”
“Full of these ideas I immediately employed a carpenter and smith to carry them into effect. . . . To my great delight, a piece of cloth, such as it was, was the produce. . . .”
Sadly, this first machine of Cartwright's was not at all successful, and was actually slower in its operation than a manual hand loom.
Nevertheless, it worked and proved that producing cotton cloth by mechanical means was a possibility. All Cartwright had to do now was to improve and refine the process.
It took a whole series of improvements and new patents before, finally, in 1788, his machine had reached a point where the three component processes of weaving—shedding, picking and beat-up—could be performed with sufficient speed and efficiency. . . .
stimulus.citation: “Edmund Cartwright & the Invention of the Power Loom,” Our Nottinghamshire, May 9, 2013

items.question: According to the passage, Cartwright's first power loom

choices.text: wove cloth faster than any hand loom from the start
needed a whole factory full of workers to keep it running all day
was slower than a hand loom, but proved machines could weave
was built inside a Manchester cotton mill in 1788

hints: Find the word “Sadly” in the passage.
The passage says the machine failed and succeeded at the same time. How?
items.reasoning: The first machine was slower than a hand loom, but it worked, and it proved that making cotton cloth by machine was possible. It took a series of improvements, until 1788, to make it fast enough.

items.question: Based on this passage and your knowledge of social studies, machines like the power loom moved cloth making

choices.text: from factories back into workers' homes
from Britain over to the American South
from water and steam back to hand power
from hand work at home into factories

hints: Before machines, where did spinners and weavers make cloth?
A machine needed power, a building and workers in one place. What was that place called?
items.reasoning: Before machines, spinners and weavers made cloth by hand at home: the domestic system. Machines like the power loom needed power, a building and workers in one place: the factory.
